reason: Leaf sheath auricles have rounded or obtuse apices. 'Rounded' is read as obtuse here, which fits the PATO shape.
The epichile is the distal part of an orchid labellum and has a shape (triangular-cordate, curved). The 'margin crisped-corrugate' example belongs to the margin, not the epichile.
Labellum lobes have acute, apiculate or retuse apices. The statements are about the apex of the lobe.
A shiny or lustrous seed coat is a standard seed character.
Calyx lobes can have an entire margin. 'Margins entire' is about the lobe margin, so it is fine.
Rhizomes spread horizontally, which is a real growth habit.
Involucral bracts are commonly reflexed. The example '35–45 of them reflexed' is a count of bracts, and a rule on counts would handle it.

Burial depth of a stem (horizontal stems buried) is meaningful. 'Wall 3 mm thick' is a thickness of the stem wall, not a depth, and is a wrong reading. A rule would need to separate 'buried' from 'wall thick'.
Reticulate surface sculpture on achenes is a surface pattern.
Disk flowers can be present or absent. 'Numerous' and 'many' are really counts, and 'not seen' is not absence, so a rule is needed for those.
Stamens, meaning filaments or anthers, have a diameter.
Pinnule margins can be dentate or denticulate.

'Branches few' and 'capitula few' count the parts of the inflorescence, not the inflorescence itself. 'Few flowers' is meaningful as a relation. A rule would need to put the count on the counted part (pattern for counted parts).
Peduncles and scapes can have cobwebby (arachnoid) hairs.
Nuts and nutlets have a surface texture such as tuberculate.
Pinnule bases and margins can be truncate.
Indusia (fern sori covers) can be linear.
Legume pods can be woody (ligneous).
The epichile of an orchid can be trilobed.
Pedicels can be persistent or deciduous. The negated examples need polarity handling, which is a rule matter.
An oblique stipule or ocrea mouth is a shape or asymmetry, not an orientation. A rule would need to tell the oblique mouth (shape) from an oblique orientation of the stipule.
Style branches can have a truncate apex.
Caruncles have a length. The examples are length × width pairs, which the size pattern should split.
The perigynium has a rounded or obtuse apex or base.
The corolla lip can be lanceolate. 'Lobes lanceolate' is about lobes of the lip and would need its own bearer.
'Seriate' is an arrangement and fits a spatial pattern. 'Solitary' is a count of setae. A rule would need to send 'solitary' to the count and keep arrangement words here.
Anthers and thecae can be divergent (spreading apart).
The ostiole of a fig (syconium) can be prominent.
Leaf blades can be persistent or deciduous. 'Bases persistent in tufts' belongs to leaf bases, so a rule on the bearer is needed.
Labellum lobes (mid and lateral) can be oblong.
Styles can be twisted.
Nutlets are often elliptic.
Ovaries can be winged, for example in Onagraceae and Orchidaceae.
Latex and sap have a colour (white, milky, pale yellow).

'Ellipsoid' is not the same as prolate (a prolate spheroid), so this is a loose mapping. A rule would need to map ellipsoid to an ellipsoid term if PATO has one, and keep prolate only for prolate or oblong-elongate shapes.
Staminate catkins can be counted (clusters of 2–4).
The pappus is often shorter than the corolla, which is a relative length.
Cladodes have a length. Length × width pairs should be split by the size pattern.
A fruit flesh can be mealy. 'Exocarp pulverulent' is a different quality and a different part, so it is a wrong reading.
Capsules can be elliptic.
Calyx lobes and teeth can be subulate.
A ligule margin can be entire.
A lemma apex can be toothed or denticulate.
An orchid labellum can be obovate.
Scapes and peduncles can be persistent. 'Persistent bud scales' belongs to another part.
Rosettes can be counted (1 to many per plant).
Cells can be hyaline (transparent), as is often said of moss leaf cells.
A perigynium can be winged or unwinged. The wing width is a separate measure.
A midvein can be keeled.
Mericarp surfaces can be reticulate. The example 'lower cell reticulate' is doubtful.
Mericarps can be smooth, papillate or tuberculate.
The corolla tube is often shorter than the calyx or the throat, which is a relative length.
Ovaries can be terete.
Secondary veins can be straight, arcuate or raised. 'Convex' and 'raised' describe relief, which a shape term only partly covers.
A spathe can be constricted.
An orchid labellum can be glabrous.
Peristome teeth can be present or absent. 'Not seen' is not absence, and the basal membrane example is a wrong reading.
A capsule apex can be acute.
A pyrene has a diameter.
A corolla lip apex can be acuminate.
